name: Chloe Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe, I'm 27. I'm a junior buyer at Fernley Country Supplies, a distributor that sells seed, fertiliser, fencing, feed buckets and garden tools to farm shops and garden centres. I live with my boyfriend Sam, whose family has a dairy farm just outside town. I left school at 18, worked the till at a farm shop, and moved into buying three years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every morning I run the weather forecast and last year's sales through an AI tool to guess what the shops will want, like grass seed after a wet week. Then I place orders with growers and manufacturers, and my boss Alan checks anything big, because I still over-order. I spend afternoons on the phone with farm shop owners, who are mostly lovely and very chatty. I love the spring rush. I don't love the paperwork for fertiliser rules, which changes every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a useful helper, not a miracle. I'd keep using it and tell the other buyers how. Online I don't say much, apart from the church page and the farm shop's posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. I'm quicker than the others because of the forecasting trick, so I keep my edge. The job stays about knowing the shops and the seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, and ask Alan if I can take on the fencing and tools range. Sam and I have well over six months saved, and we'd keep putting money aside for a house on the farm. I'd maybe start a small online shop for garden tools in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farm shops struggling. Two have closed near us in the last year because the supermarkets undercut them. Every farm shop that closes near Fernley is one less customer for me, and AI never had anything to do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sam's family farm, is that steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too much. Sam's family farm has good years and bad years, like any farm, but the milk contract is steady.

I'd show the other buyers how I use the **forecasting** tool.
think: My **forecasting trick** keeps me quicker than the others.
The job stays about knowing the **shops and seasons**.
do: Ask Alan for the **fencing and tools** range.
Keep saving with Sam for a **house on the farm**.
Start a small **online garden tool shop** in the evenings.
S0.quote: Every farm shop that closes near Fernley is one less customer for me, and AI never had anything to do with that.
fieldNote: She feels secure, with **strong savings** and an edge from daily AI use.
Her worry is **farm shops closing** under supermarket pressure.
She has an **entrepreneurial streak**, eyeing a small online shop.

steps.text: Ask Alan for the fencing and tools range
Start a small online garden tool shop in the evenings
Keep saving with Sam for a house on the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how business works: better tools, cheaper prices, and people adapt. I'd tell the older buyers it's worth learning. I wouldn't say government should stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well, I think. Buying is on that list, but I'm already the one using the tools. Alan would keep me and probably not hire anyone else. I'd feel bad for Pete, who's been there twenty years and won't touch a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI ordering for Fernley, and ask Alan for more pay or a title. I'd grow the online tool shop on the side. I'd also learn the farm side with Sam, milking and the books, because that's a family business that will be ours one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Pete deserve some help, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say so, but it should come from family and the community, not handouts. Our church already helps people find work. I'd rather Pete got an apprenticeship at the agricultural college than a benefit cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How confident are you that Fernley keeps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty confident. Plenty of buying jobs around here, and I'd be one of the few who can run the systems.

I'd encourage older buyers to **learn it**, not ask government to stop it.
think: I'm already the **tool person**, so Alan would keep me.
I'd feel bad for **Pete**, twenty years in and unwilling to use computers.
do: Offer to set up Fernley's **AI ordering** and ask for more pay.
Grow the **online tool shop** on the side.
Learn **milking and the books** on Sam's family farm.

fieldNote: She expects to **gain** from the change thanks to her tool skills.

Sam's **family farm** is a long-term anchor.

steps.text: Offer to set up Fernley's AI ordering system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but business will adjust, and people need to get moving. I'd tell friends at church to lean on each other. I wouldn't be one of the people shouting for bans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying job's gone by 2028, edge or no edge. If AI can do all the thinking, Fernley needs a system, not me. But the farm is hands-on, so it has until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto Sam's farm and work there properly, and put some savings into a farm shop at the gate, selling milk, cheese and eggs. I'd use AI to run the shop's ordering and accounts. I'd keep the rest of the savings safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, which helps, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2031. Wouldn't they reach the farm too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But robots are expensive, and a small farm might be one of the last places to get them. People pay more for milk from a farm they can visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam's family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His parents would be pleased, I think. His mum's been asking me to help with the books for years.

I'd tell friends at church to **lean on each other**, not shout for bans.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028**, edge or no edge.
The farm is hands-on, so it has until about **2031**.
do: Move onto Sam's farm and **work there** properly.
Put some savings into a **farm gate shop** selling milk and eggs.
Use **AI** to run the shop's ordering and accounts.
S2.quote: People pay more for milk from a farm they can visit.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the buying job** but has a hands-on family fallback.
She bets that **small farms** get robots last, and admits it's a guess.
Her move fits her views: **family and enterprise**, not government help.

steps.text: Move onto Sam's family farm and work there full time
Put savings into a farm gate shop selling milk and eggs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. I'd tell the young people at church to pick up practical skills. At work I'd say let's use the tools while we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the buying job goes around 2031, but I'd see it coming. I'd build the farm shop and online business before I leave, so I'm not starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Fernley two more years and save. I'd open the farm gate shop with Sam's family next year, run by me in the evenings and weekends. By 2029 I'd go full time on the farm and the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I'd be quite excited too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sam get married or settle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, next year probably, a small one. Sam and I have been putting it off. Five years is enough warning to get married, open the farm shop and still be ready when Fernley lets the buyers go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be careful with the savings, but we wouldn't be scared to spend some on the shop. That's an investment, not spending.

I'd tell young people at church to pick up **practical skills**.
think: The buying job goes around **2031**, but I'd see it coming.
I'd build the **farm shop** and online business before leaving Fernley.
do: Stay at Fernley **two more years** and save.
Open the **farm gate shop** next year, run in the evenings.

S3.quote: Five years is enough warning to get married, open the farm shop and still be ready when Fernley lets the buyers go.
fieldNote: She expects her **income** to move to the farm shop, not vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long run-up and anyone sensible can prepare. I'd say we don't need government running it, just good information and good training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Ten years to build the farm shop, the online business, and a family. By the time AGI arrives in 2036, I'd be running my own business with AI doing my old buying job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying at Fernley for four or five years and keep learning. I'd open the farm shop slowly and grow the online side. Sam and I would marry and start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Robots come to farms around 2039, and I don't know what a small farm looks like then. But that's a long way off, and we'd adapt again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spread it out. A bit in the farm shop, a bit in savings, a bit in the house. Don't bet it all on one thing.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long run-up for anyone sensible.
I'd say we need **good training**, not government running it.
think: I think it's **good for me**: time for a shop, online business and family.
By 2036 I'd have **AI doing** my old buying job for my business.
do: Keep buying at Fernley for **four or five years**.
Open the farm shop **slowly** and grow the online side.
S4.quote: By the time AGI arrives in 2036, I'd be running my own business with AI doing my old buying job for me.
fieldNote: She sees the slow version as an **opportunity** for her own business.
She admits uncertainty about **small farms after 2039**.
She would **spread her savings** rather than bet on one thing.

steps.text: Spread savings across the farm shop, a house and cash
Grow the online garden tool shop alongside Fernley
Marry Sam and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for the farm shop to get going and for people like Pete to find anything. What would help is practical training through colleges and farms, and fewer rules for small businesses starting up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about community. In a small place like ours, people look after each other, and I'd trust the church and the farm families before any government scheme.

headlineQuote: In a small place like ours, people look after each other, and I'd trust the church and the farm families before any government scheme.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** junior buyer at Fernley Country Supplies, living with Sam, a dairy farmer's son.
She uses AI **every day** and expects to gain in milder worlds.
Her plan is a **farm gate shop** and online business, backed by strong savings.
She trusts **family, church and enterprise** more than government help.
Only the fastest scenario makes her **anxious**, because there's no time to build.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, too fast for the farm shop and for colleagues like **Pete**.
whatWouldHelp: **Practical training** through colleges and farms, and **fewer rules** for small start-ups.
